# Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic form of heart failure characterized by left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction occurring toward the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery, in the absence of another identifiable cause [1]. The European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Working Group defines PPCM as heart failure with a LV ejection fraction (LVEF) typically below 45%, presenting in the last month of pregnancy or within five months postpartum [2]. It remains a diagnosis of exclusion and a significant contributor to maternal morbidity and mortality worldwide [3].

## Epidemiology

The incidence of PPCM varies markedly by geography, with the highest rates reported in Nigeria, Haiti, and South Africa, and lower rates in Europe and the United States [4]. In the United States, estimates range from 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 4,000 live births, with rising incidence attributed partly to advancing maternal age and increased awareness [5]. Established risk factors include advanced maternal age, multiparity, multiple gestation, pre-eclampsia, hypertensive disorders, and African ancestry [6,7]. Genetic predisposition is increasingly recognized, with overlap with familial dilated cardiomyopathy [8].

## Pathophysiology

The pathogenesis of PPCM is incompletely understood but appears multifactorial. A leading hypothesis implicates the cleavage of prolactin into a 16-kDa antiangiogenic and proapoptotic fragment by oxidative stress–activated cathepsin D [9]. Impaired antioxidant defenses, such as reduced expression of STAT3, contribute to this cascade in experimental models [9]. Vascular and angiogenic imbalance, particularly elevated soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1) released by the placenta, is a unifying mechanism linking PPCM with pre-eclampsia [10]. Genetic studies have demonstrated that truncating variants in *TTN* (titin) are present in approximately 15% of patients, mirroring findings in dilated cardiomyopathy [11,12]. Inflammation, autoimmunity, and myocarditis have also been proposed as contributors [13].

## Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis

PPCM commonly presents with symptoms of heart failure—dyspnea, orthopnea, fatigue, and peripheral edema—which may be difficult to distinguish from normal late-pregnancy physiology, often delaying diagnosis [14]. Echocardiography is the cornerstone of diagnosis, demonstrating reduced LVEF and frequently LV dilation [2]. Natriuretic peptides (BNP or NT-proBNP) are typically elevated and aid diagnosis and monitoring [15]. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging can provide accurate volumetric assessment and characterize myocardial tissue, although gadolinium is generally avoided during pregnancy [16]. A thorough exclusion of pre-existing cardiomyopathy, valvular disease, and ischemia is essential [1].

## Management

Management of PPCM follows general heart failure principles, adapted for pregnancy and lactation [17]. Before delivery, drugs such as angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are contraindicated due to fetal toxicity; beta-blockers (preferably beta-1 selective), hydralazine, and nitrates are preferred [18]. After delivery, standard guideline-directed therapy including ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists is appropriate [17]. Anticoagulation is warranted in patients with severely reduced LVEF given the heightened thromboembolic risk during the peripartum hypercoagulable state [19].

Bromocriptine, a dopamine agonist that inhibits prolactin secretion, has emerged as a disease-specific therapy supported by the prolactin hypothesis [20]. A randomized proof-of-concept trial and the multicenter German study demonstrated improved LV recovery with bromocriptine added to standard care, with concomitant anticoagulation [21,22]. However, definitive large-scale trials remain limited, and routine use is not universally endorsed [3]. For refractory cases, mechanical circulatory support and cardiac transplantation may be required [23]. Wearable cardioverter-defibrillators have been proposed to bridge the early high-risk period given the potential for myocardial recovery [24].

## Prognosis and Subsequent Pregnancies

Prognosis in PPCM is more favorable than in other cardiomyopathies, with a substantial proportion of patients recovering LV function, typically within six to twelve months [25]. Recovery rates are higher in regions with greater resources and in patients with less severe baseline LV dysfunction [26]. Predictors of poor outcome include LVEF below 30% at diagnosis, marked LV dilation, persistent dysfunction, and right ventricular involvement [27]. Black women experience worse recovery and higher mortality [28]. Subsequent pregnancies carry significant risk, particularly in women whose LV function has not normalized, with risk of relapse, worsening heart failure, and death; appropriate counseling is essential [29]. Multidisciplinary care involving cardiologists, obstetricians, and anesthesiologists improves outcomes, and registries continue to refine our understanding of natural history and optimal therapy [30].

## Conclusion

PPCM is a potentially life-threatening but frequently recoverable cardiomyopathy unique to the peripartum period. Advances in understanding its angiogenic and prolactin-mediated pathophysiology have informed novel therapies such as bromocriptine. Early recognition, prompt initiation of guideline-directed heart failure therapy, and careful counseling regarding future pregnancies remain central to optimizing maternal outcomes.
